title: Silas and the Surprise Parcel
markdown:
Wizard Silas lived in a house tucked into Whisperwind Mountain: a cozy burrow of bubbling beakers, tall book-piles, whirring gadgets. His constant shadow was Noir, a raven so black he seemed to drink the light, bead-eyes that noticed everything. Silas loved orderly life. Enchanted quill standing straight. Emergency mushroom soup in a perfectly labelled jar.

One breezy afternoon he was sorting interesting pebbles by size and colour, of course. A playful gust zipped through the open window, carrying a tiny rolled message that buzzed with a tickly feeling. Whiskers twitching, fingers a bit shaky, he unrolled it. Urgent. Parcel must reach Moonpetal Meadows by moonrise. MOST important. — Grizelda.

A familiar flutter in his tummy, tiny butterflies that did not need a name. He always fretted about plans unravelling, messes he could not tidy. The sun was already sinking, oranges and purples. Moonrise much too soon.

“Moonpetal Meadows, Noir.” Voice tight as a new shoelace. “Before the moon peeks out fully. Grizelda’s parcels are very important. When she says most important, she means it.” Noir ruffled dark feathers, a silent knowing. Outside: waterfalls singing to the wind, steep winding paths into misty valleys. Beautiful. Not Silas’s quiet ordered home.

The paths were slick with green moss, air cool and damp, wet earth and old stone. Along a narrow ledge the wind tugged his robes like playful fingers. A happy tune floated up. On a sunlit rock a little elf sat with a gleaming lute, playing a lively song that sounded like their own adventure, bouncy, expectant.

“And here comes Silas, the wonderfully tidy wizard, and his clever raven Noir, on their grand trip to Moonpetal Meadows! A tale that will soon be sung everywhere!”

Silas blinked behind his spectacles. “Grand? We’ve only just begun!” Noir’s soft caw was quiet amusement. The elf winked, eyes bright as dewdrops. “Your grand reputation travels far! Everyone knows how precise you are!” Another cheerful note. Silas adjusted his spectacles. “If you’re going to be mysterious, you could at least be on time about it.” The elf smiled, a twinkle that knew more than he let on. “Stories don’t wait, not even for a punctual wizard. They have a way of happening.” The music nudged them forward.

Later, a deep gorge swallowing light. Below, glow-worms like fallen stars, their soft shine in rushing water. Wondrous. The path grew steeper. Silas, usually so steady on carefully chosen routes, stumbled. He grabbed a loose stone, heart thumping wild. Losing control: the messy unexpected world. He almost froze, a whisper of turning back to the neat burrow. Noir landed on his shoulder, beak at his ear, quiet and firm.

At last the ground smoothed, air sweet. Pale shimmering flowers under the rising moon: Moonpetal Meadows. A tiny gnome, no taller than Silas’s knee, waited by the largest most radiant blooms. Silas held out the humming parcel. Long pale fingers took it; the curious hum faded. Relief, a little excitement. They had made it, just in time. “A job well done,” he whispered to Noir, a real smile.

As they turned, his hand brushed his belt and found lightness. His favourite magnifying glass—smoothly carved ebony handle, for moss and tiny flowers—was gone. He remembered setting it on a high rock when he’d helped Noir over loose stones. He looked back. Thick mist rolling, the rock obscured, too far to reach safely before the moon climbed too high. Sharp disappointment. Favourite. Ages to find. But the moon was climbing, home waiting. “It’s just a thing, Noir,” he said, though his voice felt empty. He touched the empty belt, memory of cool wood. Eyes a little wet.

The climb back felt longer. Long dancing shadows, waterfalls like hushed warnings. His hand kept reaching for the belt. Noir flew ahead, dark against moonlit sky, soft reassuring calls in the growing dark.

Home, he began tidying: scrolls that had tipped, a wobbly retort stand. Something felt different. When Noir nudged a glossy feather toward him, Silas did not feel the usual urge to file it in the box labelled Noir’s Best Feathers. He smiled, tucked it in his pocket, a small real reminder of the unplanned road. The elf’s song, the lost glass, the gnome’s fading hum—they had brought him and Noir closer without being asked. He ruffled sleek feathers, a simple warm hug, not a placement. The house was still neat, books in tidy towers. Silas himself felt a little less tied to perfect order. Outside, the wind whistled around the mountain home, and for the first time he found its unpredictable song rather wonderful, a tune he did not have to label or jar.
audience: children aged 9-10, amusing mountain fantasy adventure for independent readers
